stickers.text: Throughout the notes, two fundamentally important areas are not addressed separately: 1) the very purpose of microcontroller-based devices; 2) the structure of waves. We can assume that these are known, but that does not rule out briefly providing information about them to preserve the logic of the presentation, which is lost without this information.

dictionary.definition: a method of examining heart function based on recording its electrical activity. As the heart functions, electrical processes create a small potential difference between different areas of the body's surface. An electrocardiograph measures changes in this difference over time and records them as a graph—an electrocardiogram. An electrocardiogram can be used to determine the rate and rhythm of heart contractions, identify disturbances in the heart's electrical conduction, and detect signs of some heart diseases.

a device that measures the change in electric potential difference between two points on the body and records it as an electrocardiogram through a single measurement channel. It allows the rate and rhythm of heart contractions to be assessed and some disturbances in heart function to be identified.

an electronic device that measures electrical voltage at specified time intervals, determines which of the available levels it corresponds to, and records the result as a binary number for subsequent processing and storage.

a laboratory system on which an artificially reproduced ECG signal is used to assemble, configure, and test an electrocardiograph, comparing the measurement results with known signal characteristics without connecting the device to a person.

a small electronic device that executes a program stored in its memory, receives data from connected components, processes the data, and controls the components' operation; in our ECG device, the microcontroller controls the ADC, receives measurement results, and organizes their storage and transmission.

blocks.title: Moving from ways of studying the heart to studying electrical activity
blocks.html:
The functioning of the heart manifests itself in electrical, mechanical, acoustic, and other processes. By obtaining information about these manifestations, we can assess the condition of the heart and identify disturbances in its function.

One way to obtain this information is to record the electrical activity of the heart—an electrocardiogram (ECG). However, the medical purpose requires not only reliable information but also ensuring the person's safety.

blocks.title: Moving from the electrical activity of the heart to an electrical signal
blocks.html:
The heart contracts regularly to pump blood around the body. Each contraction is triggered by an electrical impulse that arises in specialized heart cells and spreads through the heart muscle.

When an electrical impulse passes through heart cells, charged particles—ions—move through their membranes. This changes the distribution of electric charges. Since different areas of the heart do not receive the impulse at the same time, electric fields and currents arise between them.

Human body tissues conduct electricity, so the electrical activity of the heart also manifests itself on the skin's surface. Small differences in electric potential arise at different points on the skin and change as the heart functions.

The ECG measures the difference between these potentials over time, making it possible to obtain information about the electrical activity of the heart.

stickers.title: Comment on the AI version
stickers.text:
The AI produces these two paragraphs: “The activity of heart cells is accompanied by the movement of electrically charged particles, which gives rise to electric currents and changes in electric potentials.

These changes spread through the body's tissues and create a small electric potential difference between different areas of the skin's surface.”

Here we see a common AI error—inconsistent concepts. In the first paragraph, we are told about movement that creates a current, which also leads to changes in potentials. The second paragraph says “these changes...” Which changes? Changes in electric potentials? Possibly, but then the second paragraph boils down to “changes in potentials create a potential difference.” 

In fact, somewhat surprisingly, this is also often how it is written in the textbooks on which the AI was trained.

blocks.title: Studying the electrical signal by measuring electrical voltage
blocks.html:
The electrical activity of the heart creates a potential difference between different areas of the skin's surface. To measure this difference, it is necessary to obtain an electrical signal from two points on the body and compare their potentials.

For this purpose, conductive contacts are placed on selected areas of the skin, through which electric potentials reach two inputs of the measuring device. The device determines the difference between these potentials and records how it changes over time.

Such conductive contacts are called electrodes, and measuring the potential difference between specified points on the body is called one ECG lead.

However, the measured voltage is very small, usually on the order of millivolts, and can be distorted by electrical interference. This creates a need for a device capable of accurately measuring such a weak signal.

blocks.title: Amplifying the ECG signal
blocks.html:
Through two electrodes, electric potentials from different areas of the skin reach the inputs of the measuring device. It determines the difference between these potentials, which changes as the heart functions. However, this difference is very small—usually on the order of one millivolt—so it is difficult to measure accurately in the presence of electrical interference.

In addition, electrical interference arises along with it and can distort the measurement results.

To accurately record changes in the electrical activity of the heart, it is necessary to amplify the desired signal and suppress interference. For this purpose, a device is used that amplifies the difference between the voltages at two inputs while suppressing interference that is the same at both inputs. Such a device is called a differential amplifier.

However, the amplified signal remains a continuous electrical signal. To record, store, and subsequently analyze it, it must be converted into digital form.

blocks.title: We convert the ECG signal to digital form
blocks.html:
Amplification makes it possible to measure a weak ECG signal, but to store it and analyze it later, the changes in voltage must be represented as numbers.

An analog-to-digital converter (ADC) is used for this purpose. It measures voltage at specified time intervals and converts the resulting values to digital form.

According to the technical specification, for the initial device we choose a sampling rate of 500 Hz and an ADC resolution of at least 16 bits.

The changes in the electrical activity of the heart are now represented by a sequence of numbers. However, to obtain a cardiogram, these values must be stored and used to reconstruct how the signal changes over time.

The more levels there are, the smaller the voltage changes that can be distinguished, although the actual measurement accuracy also depends on noise and interference.

The electrodes, amplifier, ADC, and power source now form an interconnected electrical system that provides a digital ECG signal.

blocks.title: The need to ensure human safety arises

We have created a method for measuring the ECG signal in which electrodes connect the human body to an electronic system with its own power source.

However, in the event of a fault, a breakdown of insulation, or connection to an external power supply, this connection can cause dangerous electric current to pass through the human body.

At the same time, the medical purpose requires not only obtaining reliable information about the heart but also ensuring human safety.

Thus, creating an ECG measurement method gives rise to an opposing process—ensuring human safety. Obtaining the signal requires electrical interaction with the body, but safety requires limiting this interaction and preventing dangerous effects.

blocks.title: The opposing process—ensuring human safety
blocks.html:
Ensuring human safety is aimed at preventing harm to a person's health and life. This process exists independently of ECG measurement.

Electric current passing through the human body can disrupt muscle function, breathing, and heart function. For example, alternating current of about 1 mA can already be felt, while current of tens of milliamperes can pose a serious danger. The risk depends on the current's magnitude, its path, and the duration of exposure.

ECG records the electrical activity of the heart but is not intended to deliver current into the body. However, if the device malfunctions, its electrical connection to a person can create a dangerous leakage current. Ensuring safety therefore requires preventing dangerous electrical effects, up to and including refusing to connect an unsafe device.

At the same time, preserving human health requires timely detection of heart disease. ECG makes it possible to detect disturbances in heart rhythm and conduction, helping a doctor make medical decisions.

Thus, ensuring human safety both prevents the use of a potentially dangerous electrical device and requires obtaining information about heart function, including through ECG.

blocks.title: Creating and checking a training test bench (TTB)
We assemble a training test bench (TTB)
blocks.html:
Medical use of ECG requires measuring the electrical activity of the heart. However, a device whose safety has not yet been checked must not be connected to a person.

We therefore create a training test bench (TTB) on which, instead of a person, we use an ECG simulator—a device that reproduces the heart's electrical signal with known characteristics.

We connect the simulator to the ADS1292ECG-FE measurement board through the provided laboratory interface, and the board to a computer. We set the heart rate to 60 beats per minute, the amplitude to 1 mV, and the sampling rate to 500 Hz. We obtain a recording lasting 10–30 seconds and compare it with the original signal.

Thus, the TTB makes it possible to create and check an ECG measurement method without exposing a person to danger from an untested device. At the same time, successful measurement on the test bench does not yet confirm the electrical safety of the future device.

Since the source of a real ECG signal is the electrical activity of the heart, this activity must be reproduced artificially on the training test bench. For this purpose, we use an ECG simulator that creates a varying voltage corresponding to a particular model of cardiac activity.

We choose a simulator that allows us to set the heart rate, amplitude, and signal shape. We can now reproduce identical electrical signals and check the results of their measurement.

But reproducing a signal does not yet mean recording it. This requires a device capable of measuring small changes in voltage.

The resulting values are received by the MSP430F5529 microcontroller installed on the board, which controls conversion and data transmission.

We can now turn changes in voltage into a sequence of numbers. To observe and check the results, we need to transmit them to a computer.

blocks.html:
The ADC determines individual voltage values, but the medical information lies in how the electrical signal changes over time. Individual measurements must therefore be combined into a continuous sequence.

In the software, we open Analysis → Scope, select the first channel and start acquiring data using Acquire. We observe how successive digital values form an ECG graph.

First, we make a recording lasting 10 seconds. At a rate of 500 Hz, it should contain 5000 samples. We then increase the duration to 30 seconds, obtaining 15 000 samples.

We check for interruptions and data loss.

We have now obtained a cardiogram of an artificial signal. But to check its accuracy, we need to save the results.

blocks.title: Saving the measured data
blocks.html:
The resulting cardiogram shows how the electrical signal changes, but after the measurement is complete, the results must be saved so that they can be checked and processed again.

To do this, we go to the Save tab in the software. First, we save the digital ADC values using Data – Codes. We then save the values converted to electrical voltage using Data – Volts.

Since the measurement result depends on the device settings, we also save the contents of its registers using Register Setting. In addition, we record the specified simulator parameters and the test duration.

The supplied software allows these data to be exported as XLS files.

The original signal and its measurement result can now be compared independently of the test bench's operation.

blocks.title: Checking the results of the training test bench's operation
blocks.html:
We have created an artificial ECG signal, measured it and saved the result. However, to confirm that the test bench is working properly, we need to establish how closely the measurement matches the original signal.

We open the saved data and compare the measured amplitude with the specified value of 1 mV. We then determine the intervals between recurring cardiac cycles and check that they correspond to a rate of 60 beats per minute.

We analyze the signal shape, the number of samples, the noise level and the stability of the measurement in repeated tests. We also check how the system responds to simulated electrode disconnection, if the equipment provides such a mode.

If deviations are found, we identify their causes, adjust the settings and repeat the measurement.

As a result, we obtain a laboratory test bench on which an ECG signal can be reproduced and its recording checked without involving a person.

However, successful operation of the test bench does not yet prove that the future medical device is safe. We now need to move on to building its own measurement signal chain.

blocks.title: Building the measurement signal chain of a single-channel ECG device
Moving from an artificial signal to the electrical activity of the heart
blocks.html:
On the training test bench, we measured a signal generated by a simulator. In reality, however, the ECG signal arises from the electrical activity of the heart and propagates through the body's tissues.

The measurement conditions are therefore more complex: electric potentials on the skin surface are very small, depend on the location of the measurement points and are accompanied by interference.

For the future device to obtain this information, we need to determine between which points on the body the electric potential difference will be measured.

This creates the need to establish one ECG lead—a particular way of recording the potential difference between areas of the body.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Establishing one ECG lead
blocks.html:
The electrical activity of the heart creates different potentials on the surface of the body. However, an individual potential value does not yet constitute a measurable ECG signal: the potential difference between two points must be determined.

For this purpose, we select lead I, which compares the electric potentials recorded from the right and left arms. The change in this difference over time forms the signal of one lead.

Thus, recording requires obtaining two electric potentials and comparing them. A single-channel ECG device has one measurement channel, although it uses two measurement contacts.

But the electric potentials exist on the skin surface, while the electronic device is separate from the person. This creates the need for elements through which these potentials can reach the measurement system.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Electrodes appear
blocks.html:
To measure the potential difference between areas of skin, we need to enable interaction between the body surface and the measurement device.

For this purpose, we provide electrodes—special conductive elements intended to record the body's electric potentials.

However, the contact between an electrode and the skin is not ideal: its electrical properties depend on the material, the condition of the skin, movement and the quality of the contact. This can distort the weak ECG signal.

We therefore select electrodes with established electrical characteristics and confirmed biocompatibility for the future medical device.

During development, we reproduce electrode–skin interaction on the TTB using a laboratory equivalent of the electrical contact, without connecting the device to a person.

The electrodes now make it possible to obtain the signal, but it still needs to be transmitted to the measurement electronics.

blocks.title: Enabling signal transmission from the electrodes
blocks.html:
Electrodes allow potentials to be recorded, but the measurement electronics must receive them without significant distortion.

Electrodes record electric potentials on the skin surface, but the measurement device is located some distance from them. To transmit these potentials to the device inputs, we connect each electrode to the corresponding input using an insulated conductor. We combine the conductors into a cable intended to connect the electrodes to the electrocardiograph. This cable is called a patient cable.

Its conductors transmit weak electrical signals, but they can also pick up electromagnetic interference and create additional distortion during movement.

When designing the cable, we therefore consider its electrical characteristics, protection against interference, mechanical strength and connection reliability.

On the TTB, we check how the cable affects the reproduced signal, using a compatible laboratory interface instead of connecting a person.

The signal can now pass from the electrodes to the measurement device. However, interference and unwanted electrical effects can be transmitted along with the useful signal and must be limited.

blocks.title: Reproducing electrode–skin contact conditions
blocks.html:
On the TTB, the simulator creates a signal with known characteristics. In an actual measurement, however, additional electrode–skin contact resistance appears between the electrical activity of the heart and the device input.

This resistance can differ between electrodes and change as the person moves. As a result, the measured signal is distorted and the influence of electrical interference increases.

We therefore add an electrode–skin contact equivalent to the TTB—a laboratory model that allows different electrical resistances and contact-related distortions to be reproduced.

We check how much changes in contact conditions affect the resulting cardiogram.

The TTB now allows us to investigate not only the simulator's ideal signal, but also the conditions under which it is transmitted to the measurement electronics. This reveals the need to protect the measurement input and improve its robustness.

blocks.title: Creating protection for the measurement input
blocks.html:
The measurement input must detect very weak electrical signals. However, unwanted electrical effects can also be transmitted through it in the event of faults.

Input protection must therefore be provided between the external electrode interface and the sensitive measurement electronics to limit hazardous effects and prevent component damage.

When developing a medical device, we take into account leakage current limits, electrical insulation requirements and the protection against defibrillator effects specified in the technical specification.

However, the protective components themselves can change the characteristics of the measured signal. They must therefore be designed to provide safety while preserving measurement accuracy.

The specific medical protection circuit is developed and checked separately. For now, we investigate its influence on the TTB only using specialized test signals.

inline_notes.text: the passage through the human body of a brief, powerful electrical pulse delivered by a defibrillator to restore normal heart rhythm; if an electrocardiograph is connected at that moment, the pulse can reach its measurement inputs, so the device must have special protection.

blocks.title: Separating the useful ECG signal from electrical interference
blocks.html:
Input protection limits hazardous effects but does not eliminate interference that may be present along with the useful ECG signal.

Electrical effects that appear in a similar way at both measurement inputs are particularly significant and are called common-mode interference.

To extract the useful signal, we determine the voltage difference between the inputs and suppress their common component (differential measurement).

The ability to suppress such interference is characterized by the CMRR coefficient. The higher it is, the better the measurement system separates the useful signal from common-mode interference.

On the TTB, we check the effect of identical interference on both inputs and save the measurement results.

More reliable measurement of the weak signal now becomes possible, but a specialized electronic component that combines these capabilities is needed.

blocks.title: Selecting the ADS1291 measurement chip
blocks.html:
On the training test bench, we used a ready-made ADS1292ECG-FE board. However, to create our own portable device, we need to transfer measurement from the laboratory board to the electronic circuit being developed.

Since one ECG lead is required, we select the ADS1291—a specialized chip with one measurement channel, a programmable amplifier and a 24-bit ADC.

It is intended to record weak biopotentials and allows gain, measurement rate and electrode lead-off detection to be configured.

We use the technical documentation and the manufacturer's recommended solutions as the basis for the design.

The signal amplification and conversion functions are now combined in one chip. However, to record correctly, we need to determine its operating parameters.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Setting the ECG signal gain
blocks.html:
The ADS1291 allows the electrical signal to be amplified before conversion to digital form. But too little gain makes it difficult to use the available measurement range, while excessive gain can overload the input signal chain.

We therefore select the gain of the PGA—the programmable amplifier built into the ADS1291.

The chip supports gains of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12. For the initial test, we select a suitable value, taking into account the input voltage range and possible signal offset.

On the TTB, we apply signals of different amplitudes and check whether their shape is preserved without overload or significant distortion.

The weak ECG signal is now matched to the converter's measurement range, but we need to ensure that it is recorded sequentially over time.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Configuring analog-to-digital conversion
blocks.html:
Amplification allows the electrical signal to be prepared for measurement, but further recording requires its digital values to be obtained continuously.

For this purpose, we configure the ADS1291's built-in 24-bit ADC for a sampling rate of 500 Hz. Every 2 milliseconds, the converter should produce a new measured voltage value.

We set the rate through the CONFIG1 register and the measurement channel parameters through CH1SET.

After each conversion is complete, the chip generates the DRDY data-ready signal. The result can be obtained through the SPI digital interface.

We check on the TTB that the converter outputs successive values at the specified rate and without overload.

The measurement signal chain now produces digital samples of the ECG signal. However, the samples themselves do not yet show whether reliable contact with the measurement electrodes is maintained.

blocks.title: Enabling electrode lead-off detection
blocks.html:
The measurement system converts the incoming signal into digital values. However, if electrode–skin contact is disrupted, interference may be recorded instead of a reliable ECG.

We therefore use the Lead-off Detection function provided in the ADS1291—electrode lead-off detection.

It allows signs of disrupted electrical contact to be identified from the state of the measurement input. The chip provides special test modes whose parameters are set by control registers.

On the TTB, we reproduce a working connection and its interruption using laboratory equipment, checking that these states are detected correctly.

The device is now capable not only of obtaining an ECG signal, but also of detecting one of the causes of its unreliability.

However, the characteristics of the measurement signal chain also depend on how its components are placed and connected on the electronic board.

blocks.title: Designing the printed circuit board for the measurement signal chain
blocks.html:
We have determined the components and functions of the measurement signal chain, but for them to work together, the components must be placed on a single printed circuit board.

The weak ECG signal is sensitive to electrical interference arising in digital and power supply circuits. The board design must therefore preserve signal quality.

We use KiCad or a similar system for the design. We place the ADS1291, the supporting components specified by the manufacturer, the measurement input circuits and the digital data transmission interface.

We separate sensitive analog connections from sources of interference, provide the necessary power supply decoupling and follow the layout requirements for the measurement section.

The resulting design must be checked against the ADS1291 documentation and electrical safety requirements before the medical version is manufactured.

The individual components now form the future ECG device's own measurement signal chain.

blocks.title: Checking our own measurement signal chain
blocks.html:
Our own measurement board must perform the same basic operations that we previously tested on the ADS1292ECG-FE. However, changes to the design may affect measurement accuracy and interference levels.

We therefore return to the training test bench and use the known parameters of the artificial ECG signal.

We test our own measurement chain using the internal test signal and, after preparing a compatible test interface, using an external simulator. We compare the amplitude, signal shape, measurement frequency and noise level with the results from the laboratory board.

We also test resistance to interference, amplifier operation, the absence of overload and electrode lead-off detection.

If the results do not meet the established requirements, we identify the causes and adjust the design.

Now we can evaluate not only individual components, but also the result of their combined operation in our own measurement chain.

blocks.title: Completing the measurement chain
blocks.html:
We have moved from laboratory measurement of an artificial signal to developing our own measurement chain for a single-channel ECG device.

The electrode interface makes it possible to acquire electric potentials, the input circuits must limit hazardous effects, and the ADS1291 amplifies the signal and converts it into digital values.

Now the acquisition of reliable information and the provision of electrical safety determine the structure of a single measurement system.

However, the measurement chain itself is not yet a standalone electrocardiograph. For continuous operation, it needs a stable electrical power supply, a control device, and the accumulation and transmission of digital samples.

Further assembly therefore requires integrating the measurement chain with the power supply and digital control system. The safety of connecting it to a person remains subject to subsequent independent verification.

blocks.title: Creating the power supply and digital control system for a single-channel ECG device
Creating a measurement control system
blocks.html:
The ADS1291 measurement chip converts the ECG signal into digital values. However, it cannot, by itself, organize the saving of an examination, manage data transmission or interact with the user.

This requires a small programmable device that controls the operation of electronic components, called a microcontroller.

We choose the ESP32-S3, which supports digital interfaces, Bluetooth LE and Wi-Fi. For initial tests, we use a ready-made ESP32-S3 development board, while the final design provides for placing the corresponding module on our own board.

The measurement chain can now become part of a controlled system. However, this requires data exchange between the ADS1291 and the microcontroller.
blocks.author: ai_edited

blocks.title: Connecting the measurement chain to the microcontroller
blocks.html:
The ADS1291 produces digital values of the measured voltage, and the ESP32-S3 must receive them for further processing. For the two devices to exchange information, their method of transmitting digital data must be coordinated.

For this, we use SPI—a serial communication interface for electronic components.

The SCLK signal provides the clock pulses for the exchange, DIN receives commands from the microcontroller, DOUT transmits measurement results, and CS allows the ADS1291 to be selected for communication. On the ESP32-S3 side, these signals correspond to the SPI CLK, MOSI, MISO and Chip Select lines.

We also connect the DRDY output to a microcontroller input capable of handling interrupts. Through DRDY, the converter reports that a new measurement is ready. The START and PWDN/RESET signals allow control of ADC startup and reset.

The ESP32-S3 can now control the converter and receive its data. However, correct communication depends on the compatibility of the electrical characteristics of both devices.

blocks.title: Matching the electrical characteristics of the components
blocks.html:
We have established digital communication between the ADS1291 and the ESP32-S3, but identical interface names alone do not guarantee correct interaction.

The ESP32-S3 microcontroller is designed for a supply voltage of about 3.3 V. The ADS1291 has separate analog supply circuits, AVDD, and digital supply circuits, DVDD. According to the documentation, the permissible digital supply voltage for the ADS1291 is 1.7–3.6 V, and the analog supply voltage is 2.7–5.25 V.

For the laboratory version, we therefore choose compatible digital logic levels and check that the signals from one device do not exceed the permissible voltages of the other. If the digital section of the ADS1291 operates from 1.8 V, logic-level matching with the ESP32-S3 will be required.

In this way, the digital connection becomes not just a physical link, but a coordinated interaction between two devices.

However, even with a correct connection, the controller must receive data precisely when it is ready.

blocks.title: Coordinating the timing of data acquisition
blocks.html:
The ADS1291 must perform 500 measurements every second, but the ESP32-S3 also controls other electronic processes at the same time. Data acquisition therefore cannot depend solely on software delays in the microcontroller.

For this, we use the DRDY signal, which reports the completion of the next conversion.

When DRDY arrives, the microcontroller starts reading the result through SPI and assigns it a sequence number. Each sample corresponds to the next point in time at which the signal is recorded.

At a frequency of 500 Hz, the interval between samples is 2 milliseconds. We check on the TTB that the microcontroller manages to acquire the data and does not miss data-ready events.

The measurement chain and the controller now operate with coordinated timing. However, subsequent data processing and transmission may take longer than acquiring a new sample.

blocks.title: Ensuring continuous accumulation of measurements
blocks.html:
The microcontroller receives new ECG values every 2 milliseconds. However, processing and transmission of the previous data may still be underway when the next sample arrives.

To prevent these processes from interfering with each other, we organize a memory area in the ESP32-S3 in which new data is written sequentially, while the data already accumulated is read for further processing (a circular buffer).

We assign each sample a sequence number that allows missing measurements to be detected.

A recording lasting 30 seconds at a frequency of 500 Hz requires 15 000 samples to be saved. At three bytes per sample, the raw values will occupy 45 000 bytes, not including auxiliary information.

New measurements can now continue to be acquired independently of the processing of previously acquired data.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Ensuring measurements are preserved
blocks.html:
The circular buffer allows the ECG signal to be accumulated temporarily, but the contents of RAM may be lost when power is switched off.

We therefore provide for saving completed examinations in memory that retains information after the device is switched off (nonvolatile memory).

For the initial prototype, we can use the built-in Flash memory of the ESP32-S3 module, first allocating an area for examinations. Along with the samples, we save the measurement parameters, recording time and indicators of detected errors.

Results can now be stored in the device itself, even without a connection to a computer.

However, continuous recording and saving of data require stable operation of all the electronics, which depends on the electrical power supply.

blocks.title: Ensuring a stable electrical power supply
blocks.html:
Combining the ADS1291 and the ESP32-S3 allows digital measurements to be acquired and saved, but both devices can operate correctly only at certain supply voltages.

The ESP32-S3 is particularly sensitive to insufficient power, and its consumption increases during wireless communication.

Therefore, for the digital system we provide a regulated 3.3 V supply. According to Espressif's recommendations, the ESP32-S3 power supply must provide a current of at least 500 mA.

At the laboratory stage, we use the development board's power supply as specified by the manufacturer. We check voltage stability during controller startup, data acquisition and operation of the wireless module.

The digital system can now operate stably. However, a stable power supply for the controller does not yet guarantee accurate measurement of the weak ECG signal.

blocks.title: Separating the low-noise power supply for the measurement chain
blocks.html:
The ESP32-S3 consumes electrical energy unevenly. Changes in consumption can create interference in the power supply circuits, which can reach the sensitive input of the ADS1291.

The power supply for the measurement chain must therefore be low-noise. For the analog section, we provide separate filtering and a low-noise voltage regulator (LDO).

In the design, we aim for a nominal analog supply voltage for the ADS1291 of about 3 V. For its digital section, we choose a voltage compatible with the ESP32-S3 interface.

In accordance with TI's recommendations, near the ADS1291 power supply circuits we provide decoupling capacitors, including 0.1 μF and 10 μF, and arrange the return currents so that digital interference does not pass through the sensitive analog section.

The power supply now supports not only the operation of the electronics, but also measurement quality.

blocks.title: Testing the effect of digital electronics on measurement
blocks.html:
Separate power supply filtering reduces electrical interference, but the microcontroller can also affect the measurement chain through digital connections and electromagnetic radiation.

Therefore, when designing the board, we place sensitive analog circuits away from the ESP32-S3 radio module and high-frequency digital lines. We pay particular attention to the ADS1291 measurement inputs.

On the TTB we record the same artificial ECG signal, first with minimal digital activity, then with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi operating.

We compare the noise level, signal shape and number of lost samples.

This is how we check whether digital control reduces measurement reliability. However, medical use requires the device to operate without a permanent connection to an external power supply.

blocks.title: Moving to self-contained power
blocks.html:
On the training test bench, power can come from a laboratory power supply, but a portable electrocardiograph must operate independently.

We therefore provide a rechargeable battery module capable of supplying energy to the measurement chain, controller and data transmission equipment.

For the prototype, we choose a ready-made protected rechargeable battery module with a compatible power management system. This allows us to avoid developing a battery-cell protection circuit ourselves.

We determine the capacity after measuring the device's consumption during ECG recording, data saving and wireless communication. The technical specification provides for independent operation, but its duration has not yet been defined.

The measurement system can now operate without a permanent connection to an external power supply. However, the energy stored in the battery is gradually used up, so provision must be made for replenishing it safely.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Providing charging through USB-C
blocks.html:
The rechargeable battery enables independent operation of the ECG device, but after discharging it must receive electrical energy from an external source.

According to the technical specification, we provide USB-C for this purpose. Charging is managed by a dedicated controller matched to the selected protected rechargeable battery module.

However, connecting a USB cable creates a new connection to external electrical equipment. For a medical device, this requires separate consideration of electrical safety.

In the initial design, we therefore provide separate charging and measurement modes: ECG recording is blocked when the charging cable is connected. The possibility of combining these modes can be considered only after the corresponding protection has been designed and tested.

The battery can now replenish its energy reserve without turning laboratory debugging into a test on a person.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Monitoring the power supply status
blocks.html:
The rechargeable battery allows the device to operate independently, but its voltage changes as it discharges. If the power supply becomes insufficient, the electronic components may stop performing measurements correctly.

We therefore add monitoring of the battery status and supply voltages.

The microcontroller must receive information about the charge level and detect an insufficient-power condition. To protect against unstable operation, we use the Brownout Detection mechanism provided in the ESP32-S3, which responds to a drop in voltage.

If permissible conditions are violated, the device must stop recording, mark the examination as incomplete and not present the acquired data as a reliable ECG.

Thus, ensuring safety extends not only to electrical effects on a person, but also to the reliability of information acquired under changing power supply conditions.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Coordinating the startup of all electronic components
blocks.html:
After power is switched on, the electronic components do not begin operating simultaneously. The microcontroller may start before the power supply and internal measurement circuits of the ADS1291 have stabilized.

If recording begins too early, the results may be unreliable.

We therefore establish a specific startup sequence. First, the ADS1291 power supply and clock circuits must stabilize, then the converter is reset and configured in accordance with the manufacturer's documentation.

The ESP32-S3 checks the availability of the ADS1291, writes the required settings, reads them back for verification and starts an internal test measurement.

Only after a successful check does the system enter the ready state.

Switching on the power now becomes the start of a controlled measurement preparation procedure, rather than simply switching on all the components.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Creating recording controls and status indication
blocks.html:
The measurement chain and controller can start automatically and acquire data. However, the user needs to know whether the device is ready to operate, whether recording is in progress, and whether an error has occurred.

For this purpose, we provide a button to start and stop recording, connected to a digital input of the ESP32-S3.

To make the device's actions visible, we add indicator lights. They must distinguish between readiness for measurement, recording in progress, low battery charge, and a fault.

If a power supply or measurement chain error is detected, the device must not indicate normal recording status.

The user can now control the device and receive information about its status. It remains to check how all the electronic processes we have created interact when carrying out a complete study.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Checking how the power and control systems work together
blocks.html:
We have combined the ADS1291 measurement chain, the ESP32-S3 microcontroller, the power supply system, data accumulation, and the controls.

However, the operability of individual components does not yet mean that the entire system works correctly.

We therefore return to the training test bench and reproduce an ECG signal with known parameters. We start the device, check ADS1291 initialization, and perform a 30-second recording at a rate of 500 Hz.

We check that 15 000 consecutive samples are received and saved, with no unrecorded losses. We repeat the test under various modes of digital activity and permissible battery power conditions.

We separately check the device's response to loss of communication, insufficient power, and a restart.

As a result, we obtain a controllable, self-contained measurement system capable of recording and saving an artificial ECG signal.

However, for the ECG device to function fully, it needs a program that will sequentially control all these actions, process the signal, and determine the study results.

blocks.title: Developing firmware, ECG signal recording, and processing
Creating a program to control the electrocardiograph
blocks.html:
The electronic components of the future ECG device are interconnected, but they must work together in a specific sequence.

For this purpose, we develop a program that runs directly on the ESP32-S3 microcontroller (firmware).

We use the C language and Espressif's ESP-IDF development environment. It allows us to control electronic interfaces, memory, and the execution of multiple software tasks.

We create a firmware project and provide separate control of the measurement chain, sample acquisition, signal processing, and saving of results.

The actions of the electronic components can now be determined by a single program. However, before starting a measurement, we need to make sure that the equipment is operational.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Organizing device startup and checks
blocks.html:
After power is applied, the microcontroller begins executing the program, but the measurement chip and other components may not yet be ready to operate.

The firmware therefore first checks the power supply status, starts the digital interfaces, and establishes communication with the ADS1291.

It then performs self-diagnostics—a check of the operability of the main electronic subsystems. If the microcontroller does not receive the expected response from the ADC, the device enters an error state and prevents recording.

If the check is completed successfully, the device enters the ready state and waits for a start command.

Starting a measurement now depends not only on switching on the power but also on confirming that the electronic system is operational.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Creating a driver for the measurement chip
blocks.html:
The microcontroller has established a connection with the ADS1291, but controlling the converter requires sending it commands in a specific format.

For this purpose, we develop an ADS1291 driver—a software module that implements communication over the SPI interface.

In ESP-IDF, we use the SPI Master driver. Before configuring the registers, we stop continuous data output with the SDATAC command (0x11). We use RREG to read registers and WREG to write them.

After changing the settings, we read them back and check that they match the specified values. For continuous recording, we provide the RDATAC command (0x10).

The microcontroller can now not only receive data but also change the ADC's operating mode. Consequently, we can set the required measurement characteristics through software.

blocks.title: Setting measurement parameters through software
blocks.html:
The ADS1291 supports various conversion modes. However, our ECG device needs to acquire one continuous signal at a specific rate and gain.

We therefore select continuous mode in the CONFIG1 register and set DR[2:0] = 010, corresponding to 500 samples per second at the standard clock frequency.

Through the CH1SET register, we set measurement of an external differential signal and the gain previously verified on the TTB.

We also configure the reference voltage source, clocking, and the necessary auxiliary functions of the ADS1291.

We save the measurement parameters in the firmware settings.

The converter now operates in a mode that meets the initial requirements of the technical specification. However, the correctness of the configured parameters must be confirmed using a known signal.

blocks.title: Checking the correctness of digital measurement
blocks.html:
Configuring the ADC through software does not yet prove that the chip correctly converts the input voltage.

We therefore first use the ADS1291's built-in test signal, which allows us to check the measurement channel without an external connection.

Through the CONFIG2 register, we enable the test source and select the periodic signal mode provided by the chip. We then start conversion and compare the resulting digital values with the expected ones.

If the results match the characteristics of the test mode, we switch the measurement input to the signal from an external ECG simulator.

We can now check conversion using both internal and external sources. However, ECG recording requires us to continuously acquire every new sample.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Acquiring samples over SPI
blocks.html:
The ADS1291 produces a new digital value every 2 milliseconds, but the microcontroller needs to be informed promptly when it is ready.

For this purpose, we use the DRDY signal. When a new measurement is available, the chip drives DRDY low, and the ESP32-S3 receives a notification through an interrupt.

A separate firmware task then reads the data over SPI. For the single-channel ADS1291, the frame contains 24 status bits and 24 bits of the measured signal, that is, 6 bytes.

The firmware separates the auxiliary data from the measurement result and assigns a sequence number to the sample.

The individual ADS1291 conversions now become a sequence of digital measurements. However, the resulting codes must be correctly interpreted as electrical voltage values.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Converting digital codes into voltage values
blocks.html:
The ADS1291 transmits the measurement result as a 24-bit signed number. However, this number does not yet directly indicate the ECG signal voltage in millivolts.

The firmware must therefore convert the received code into the physical quantity of voltage.

To do this, we account for the ADC reference voltage, the configured gain, and the range of digital values. We use the following relationship in the calculation:

U = N × Vref / ((2²³ − 1) × G),

where N is the signed digital code, Vref is the reference voltage, and G is the gain.

We convert the resulting voltage into millivolts. On the TTB, we compare it with the known amplitude of the simulator signal.

The digital samples now acquire physical meaning and can be used to plot a cardiogram.

blocks.title: Reconstructing how the ECG signal changes over time
blocks.html:
The firmware now acquires the ECG voltage in millivolts. However, the sequence of values does not yet allow us to determine when each change in the signal occurred.

For this purpose, we associate each sample with its position in time.

At a rate of 500 Hz, we take the first sample as the start of the recording; the second corresponds to 2 milliseconds, the third to 4 milliseconds, and so on. We assign a sequence number to each value.

We separately record the study's start time. If the device includes a real-time clock, we associate the entire recording with this time.

Changes in voltage can now be represented as a function of time, that is, an electrocardiogram can be plotted. However, subsequent data processing may interfere with the timely acquisition of new samples.

blocks.title: Separating measurement acquisition and processing
blocks.html:
The ADC produces a new measurement every 2 milliseconds. But calculating heart rate, filtering, and saving data may take additional time.

If all the actions are performed sequentially, the next measurement may be missed.

We therefore use the capabilities of FreeRTOS, which is included in ESP-IDF, and divide program execution into independent tasks.

After the DRDY signal, the interrupt handler notifies the data acquisition task. It reads the sample over SPI and places it in a ring buffer. Another task retrieves the accumulated values for processing.

If the buffer overflows, the firmware records an error rather than silently losing data.

Recording can now continue independently of subsequent processing, maintaining continuity of measurement.

blocks.title: Saving the original ECG signal
blocks.html:
We have learned to acquire consecutive voltage values, but subsequent digital processing will change them.

Meanwhile, for a medical study, it is important to be able to recheck exactly what the measurement chain recorded.

We therefore save the original digital ADC values separately, before applying user-defined software filters and analysis algorithms.

At the same time, we save the conversion parameters that allow the voltage to be reconstructed in physical units.

The processing results can now be compared with the original measurements. However, the original recording may contain interference that makes it difficult to assess heart function.

blocks.title: Suppressing interference through digital processing
blocks.html:
The original ECG may contain slow baseline fluctuations, power-line interference, and electrical signals from active muscles.

These effects make it difficult to extract useful information about heart function. We therefore create software-based digital filters.

For the initial display of the heart rhythm, we use band-pass filtering at approximately 0.5–40 Hz. If power-line interference is present, we provide an additional notch filter at 50 or 60 Hz.

However, filtering may change not only the interference but also the shape of the ECG itself. We therefore provide the ability to adjust and disable the filters. Full diagnostic recording will require a separately specified and verified bandwidth.

We now obtain a processed representation of the signal while retaining the original recording to check the result.

blocks.title: Detecting heartbeats
blocks.html:
After interference is reduced, it becomes easier to distinguish changes in the cardiogram that correspond to the electrical activity of the heart. However, the curve itself does not yet directly indicate the heart rate.

To determine it, we need to detect QRS complexes—characteristic sections of the ECG associated with electrical excitation of the heart's ventricles.

We develop an algorithm to find R peaks and determine the intervals between adjacent heartbeats. For this purpose, we can use the Pan–Tompkins approach, adapted to a sampling rate of 500 Hz.

We calculate heart rate (HR) from the time intervals between the detected R peaks: we divide 60 by the median of the R–R intervals expressed in seconds.

On the TTB, we check the result at simulated rates of 60, 90, and 120 beats per minute.

The digital ECG now allows us not only to observe the electrical activity of the heart but also to obtain quantitative information about its rhythm.

blocks.title: Determining the reliability of the information obtained
blocks.html:
The algorithm can detect heartbeats, but strong interference or a disruption of electrode contact can lead to an incorrect result.

It is therefore not enough simply to calculate HR—we need to determine how reliable the data underlying the calculation are.

For this purpose, we combine the ADS1291's electrode lead-off messages with software monitoring of ADC saturation, interference level, and recording continuity.

We create three quality states: GOOD—the measurement is suitable for the intended analysis, POOR—quality is reduced, INVALID—the result is unreliable.

In the INVALID state, the program must not present the calculated HR as reliable. We determine the numerical quality criteria after test bench trials.

The medical information is now accompanied by an assessment of its reliability, reducing the risk of incorrect interpretation of the results.

blocks.title: Organizing a complete ECG study
blocks.html:
The measurement system continuously acquires and processes the ECG, but practical use requires defining a specific, complete study period.

We therefore organize a recording session. When the start button is pressed, the microcontroller creates a study identifier, records the start time, and begins accumulating samples.

According to the technical specification, we provide a recording duration of 10 or 30 seconds. At a rate of 500 Hz, this corresponds to 5000 or 15 000 samples.

After the specified time has elapsed, the firmware stops recording and checks the completeness of the acquired data.

If lost samples or significant quality problems are detected, the study receives an appropriate mark.

The continuous measurement process now becomes a completed recording that can be saved and transferred for medical analysis.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Saving the study in the device's memory
blocks.html:
The completed recording is held in the microcontroller's RAM, but it may disappear when the power is turned off.

We therefore transfer the results to nonvolatile Flash memory.

To store the samples themselves, we use a dedicated memory area or a file system, such as FAT with support for Flash wear leveling. Small device settings can be saved separately through NVS.

The study must contain the original digital values, sampling rate, gain settings, recording time, and information about detected errors.

To check integrity, we add a CRC32 checksum.

The recorded ECG is now stored independently of the operation of the measurement chain. However, the saved data must remain accessible even when the device is restarted.

blocks.title: We ensure recovery from errors
blocks.html:
Failures may occur during recording: a drop in battery voltage, loss of communication with the ADC, buffer overflow, or an unexpected microcontroller restart.

If the program does not account for such situations, it may lose part of the study or save corrupted data as a complete cardiogram.

We therefore provide for error handling and restoration of the device's state.

When a fault is detected, the firmware records its cause, stops unreliable recording, and puts the device into a safe state.

After a restart, we check the saved studies using checksums. We mark incomplete recordings separately and do not present them as complete.

A failure of an electronic component or software task should now no longer lead to unnoticed distortion of medical information.

blocks.title: We prepare to transfer the digital recording to a computer
blocks.html:
The device can already create and save studies, but we need to receive them on a computer to check the results.

We therefore provide a software interface for data transfer through which the ESP32-S3 can send information about the device's state, study parameters, and saved samples.

For initial debugging, we use the USB interface provided by the board. We transmit data in packets, specifying the study number, sample positions, and error flags.

On the computer, we check that the received data match the data saved in the device.

This makes independent analysis of the results possible. However, the development of a full-featured user application and wireless transmission will be carried out in the following sections.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We test the firmware on the training test bench
blocks.html:
We have combined ADS1291 control, sample recording, signal processing, HR calculation, and study storage. However, the correct operation of individual software modules does not yet prove that the firmware works as a whole.

We therefore return to the training test bench and reproduce an ECG with known characteristics.

We check that the device records 15 000 consecutive samples in 30 seconds at a frequency of 500 Hz. We compare the measured amplitude, waveform, and calculated HR with the simulator's parameters.

We then check the effects of filtering, the handling of electrode disconnection, the absence of data loss, the saving of recordings, and recovery from software errors.

If deviations are detected, we correct the corresponding module and repeat the test.

As a result, we obtain a laboratory prototype capable of independently recording, processing, and saving an artificial ECG.

However, the results are currently accessible mainly through technical interfaces. For practical use, we need to create full-featured software that allows a person to view and analyze the cardiogram.

blocks.title: Development of computer software
We create a program for working with the electrocardiograph
blocks.html:
Our electrocardiograph can already record an electrical signal and save measurement results. However, the digital data held in the device's memory do not yet, on their own, allow a person to study the heart's activity.

To make the acquired information accessible, we create a computer application that will receive ECG data, display the cardiogram, and manage studies.

We use Python for development. Since the program must have a graphical interface with buttons, graphs, and study windows, we choose the PySide6 library, which allows us to create applications for Windows.

It is now possible to present the electrocardiograph's actions in a form the user can understand. However, we first need to test the program itself independently of the measuring device.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We test the application using an artificial ECG
blocks.html:
The computer program must display the ECG correctly, but at the initial stage its errors may become mixed with errors from the measuring device.

We therefore first create a software source of a test signal. It reproduces a previously prepared sequence of digital values corresponding to an artificial ECG.

For this, we use Python and NumPy. We prepare a test recording with a sampling rate of 500 Hz and pass it to the program in chunks, simulating the arrival of measurements from a real device.

We can now develop ECG display, storage, and processing without turning on the measurement electronics.

Once these functions have been tested, we use the same software interface to receive data from the physical device.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We create an ECG viewing window
blocks.html:
The program can already receive test ECG values, but so far they exist only as a sequence of numbers.

To observe changes in the electrical activity of the heart, we need to present these values graphically.

For this, we create a main window in the PySide6 application, and to plot the graph we use the PyQtGraph library, which is designed, among other things, for the rapid display of changing data.

On the horizontal axis, we show time in seconds; on the vertical axis, the measured voltage in millivolts. We provide for viewing one ECG lead.

The sequence of numbers now becomes a cardiogram. However, the display must be updated continuously as new measurements arrive, without interfering with their reception.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We separate data reception from cardiogram display
blocks.html:
At a sampling rate of 500 Hz, the device produces a new measurement every 2 milliseconds. However, the program window does not need to be redrawn after every sample.

Moreover, if data reception and graph updates are performed sequentially in a single thread, a display delay may disrupt signal reception.

We therefore use QThread—a mechanism for executing separate software tasks in PySide6. In the worker thread, the program receives and checks measurements, while the main thread handles the display.

We arrange for the graph to be updated through QTimer approximately 20–30 times per second. For this, we use samples that have already been accumulated, without changing their recording rate.

Displaying the cardiogram should now no longer interfere with continuous data reception.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We establish communication with the measuring device
blocks.html:
We have tested the display of an artificial signal, but the program must now receive data from the electrocardiograph we have created.

For the initial laboratory version, we use transmission through USB. In the ESP32-S3 firmware, we provide a USB CDC interface through which the device appears to the computer as a virtual serial port.

In Windows, this interface may be recognized as a COM port. To work with it, we use the Python library pyserial.

The program detects an available port, establishes a connection, and requests the device's identifier, firmware version, sampling rate, and measurement system status.

Only after checking compatibility does the program allow recording to start.

The computer and electrocardiograph can now exchange data. However, we need to determine how to distinguish measurements from service information and detect transmission errors.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We create a measurement transmission protocol
blocks.html:
The device transmits digital ECG values, but the computer must understand where a study begins, which samples belong to it, and whether any data have been lost.

We therefore develop a communication protocol—a common set of rules for forming and reading digital messages.

We assign each packet a message type, a protocol version number, a study identifier, the number of the first sample, and the number of measurements it contains.

To distinguish valid packets from corrupted ones, we add the message length and a CRC checksum. The firmware forms these packets, and the program on the computer checks their structure and integrity.

The sequence of transmitted bytes now acquires a defined meaning. However, even correctly received packets still need to be assembled into a continuous ECG recording.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We reconstruct a continuous sequence of measurements
blocks.html:
The program receives packets containing digital measurements, but data transmission may be delayed. In addition, individual packets may be lost or received more than once.

The program therefore checks the sample numbers and determines their correct sequence.

At a frequency of 500 Hz, each successive sample corresponds to a time increase of 2 milliseconds. If a gap is detected, the program marks the missing section without replacing it with invented measurements.

Data received more than once must not be recorded as new data. If the protocol provides for retransmission, the program requests the missing packets.

In this way, individual messages are used to reconstruct a continuous recording with known timing characteristics and marked disruptions.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We convert the received data into voltage
blocks.html:
The received values are digital ADC codes. But to plot the ECG, we need to know which electrical voltage corresponds to each code.

The program therefore uses the saved measurement parameters: the ADS1291 reference voltage, gain, and calibration characteristics of the measurement chain.

We convert each signed 24-bit code into voltage and express the result in millivolts (mV).

At the same time, we preserve the link between each calculated value and the original digital code. This allows the conversion to be repeated when checking the results or changing the calibration parameters.

The measurements are now represented in physical units, rather than only as numbers produced by the ADC.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We ensure correct cardiogram display
blocks.html:
We have obtained a sequence of measured voltages, but assessing the heart's activity requires not only the signal values, but also the time intervals between its changes.

We therefore display time, calculated from the sample numbers and sampling rate, on the horizontal axis of the graph, and voltage in millivolts on the vertical axis.

Using PyQtGraph, we create a sliding window, for example covering 10 seconds. At a frequency of 500 Hz, it displays 5000 samples at once. To analyze individual sections, we provide for zooming and pausing scrolling.

Changing the graph's scale must not change the saved measurements.

The program now allows us to observe the ECG waveform and examine its individual sections over time.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We display measurement status and signal quality
blocks.html:
A cardiogram may be displayed on the screen even when measurement quality has deteriorated. A graph alone is therefore insufficient for assessing the reliability of the information being received.

In section 4, we provided for monitoring electrode disconnection, interference, and missing samples. We now need to make the results of this monitoring understandable to the user.

In the interface, we display connection status, signal quality, sampling rate, and battery charge level.

If the device reports a fault or an unreliable measurement, the program displays the corresponding warning. When communication is lost, the graph stops receiving new points and displays a data gap rather than continuing to show the previous cardiogram as current.

The user now sees not only the measurement, but also the conditions under which it is performed.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We add filtering controls
blocks.html:
The acquired cardiogram may contain electrical interference that makes it difficult to observe the heart rhythm. The user therefore needs to be given the ability to choose the signal processing method.

In the program, we create settings for digital filtering. For the initial rhythm display mode, we use a range of approximately 0.5–40 Hz, and when mains interference is present, we provide for attenuation of frequencies of 50 or 60 Hz.

To implement the filters, we use the SciPy library.

However, processing can change the ECG waveform. The user can therefore switch between the original and processed signals, and the selected settings are saved with the study.

For real-time display, we apply streaming filters, while algorithms with forward-backward filtering may be used to process completed recordings.

In this way, improving the visibility of the signal does not deprive us of the ability to check its original waveform.
blocks.author: ai_checked

inline_notes.text: signal processing using mathematical calculations, in which the program changes the numerical measurement values to reduce interference and make the useful signal more distinguishable.

a reduction in the amplitude of signal oscillations at a particular frequency; for example, when processing an ECG, oscillations at a frequency of 50 Hz caused by electrical mains interference are attenuated.

blocks.title: We display heart rate
blocks.html:
The cardiogram shows the electrical activity of the heart, but to assess its rhythm, the user also needs to know the heart rate.

In section 4, we provided for detecting QRS complexes and calculating intervals between R peaks. The program now receives the results of this analysis and displays HR in beats per minute.

The value is updated as new measurements arrive. If the signal quality does not allow contractions to be detected reliably, we display a message that calculation is not possible instead of a number.

On the TTB, we compare the results with rates of 60, 90, and 120 beats per minute set on the simulator.

The cardiogram is now supplemented by a quantitative characteristic of the heart rhythm, but automatic HR calculation alone does not yet constitute a medical conclusion.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We create controls for recording a study
blocks.html:
The program allows continuous ECG viewing, but medical use requires studies of a specified duration.

We therefore add the ability to start and stop recording.

Before a study begins, the program checks that the device is ready and sends a recording command. After receiving confirmation that recording has started, it receives the study identifier and begins receiving the corresponding packets.

According to the technical specification, we provide for recordings lasting 10 or 30 seconds. We monitor their duration by the number of measured samples, rather than only by the computer's timer.

After completion, the program checks the completeness of the recording and displays the result.

An individual observation of the signal now becomes a completed study that must be saved for subsequent analysis.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We create local study storage
blocks.html:
After recording is completed, the ECG remains in the program's memory, but the data may be lost when the program is closed.

We therefore create local study storage. For this, we use SQLite—a database that runs directly on the computer.

In the database, we save the study identifier, date and time, measurement parameters, recording duration, signal quality, and location of the original sample file.

We store the measurements themselves unchanged in a separate file, preserving their link to the corresponding database record.

After saving is complete, the program checks the integrity of the file and reports the result.

The studies are now stored independently of the device's operation. However, for medical use, we need to establish which patient each recording belongs to.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: We link the study to a patient
blocks.html:
A saved ECG contains information about how the heart works, but its medical use is limited unless it is linked to a specific person.

We therefore implement patient records in the program, allowing studies to be linked to a patient identifier.

Each new study receives its own unique number and is linked to the selected patient record. The patient identifier and study number must not be the same, since one person may have many recordings.

To protect medical information, we provide access control and store personal data separately from the raw measurements.

During laboratory testing, we use only fictitious identifiers.

The results can now be combined into a history of studies for one patient, while retaining the ability to control access to them.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Creating an ECG archive
blocks.html:
We have learned to save an ECG and link it to a patient, but practical use requires access to previously performed studies.

We therefore create an ECG archive that accesses the SQLite database and displays saved recordings.

The user selects a patient, after which the program displays that patient's studies by date. When a recording is opened, the raw samples, measurement parameters and signal quality information are loaded.

The ECG is displayed on the same plot that was used for recording. This allows individual segments to be examined again and different filtering to be applied without changing the original.

Medical information is now saved not as an isolated, unlinked recording, but as a sequence of studies available for further examination.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Enabling ECG export to CSV
blocks.html:
The archive allows studies to be viewed in our program, but the data must be transferred to other applications for independent verification and mathematical analysis.

We therefore add export to CSV—a text format in which values are represented as rows and columns.

For each sample, we save its number, time in seconds, original digital ADC code, calculated voltage in millivolts and the necessary quality indicators.

We implement export using Python tools or the pandas library. We save the study metadata separately so that the measurement parameters can be restored when the file is reopened.

We check the export by importing the file again and comparing all samples with the original.

The ECG can now be studied in other programs without losing its link to the raw measurements.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Generating a medical report in PDF
blocks.html:
CSV allows the signal's numerical values to be analyzed, but for an initial review, it is more convenient for a physician to receive the ECG together with basic information about the study.

We therefore create a report in PDF format using the ReportLab library.

On the page, we place a plot of one ECG lead with the time and amplitude scales indicated. Alongside it, we list the patient identifier, date, study duration, HR, signal quality and applied filters.

We provide for the display of warnings about lost samples and other quality problems.

The report must clearly indicate if the study was performed using a simulator. We do not yet generate automated diagnostic conclusions.

The measurement results can now be presented as a document that a physician can view without a specialized program.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Enabling studies to be saved in XML
blocks.html:
PDF is convenient for reading, and CSV for numerical analysis. However, medical information systems need to receive not only a plot, but also structured information about the study.

We therefore create an export to XML—a format that allows data and their properties to be represented in a defined structure.

We use the Python module xml.etree.ElementTree. For the study, we create a structure containing identifiers, the date, recording parameters, a description of the lead, signal values and quality information.

To ensure that different programs interpret the file's contents in the same way, we specify the version of our own XML schema and check that the exported data conform to this structure.

The ECG can now be transferred in machine-readable form. However, our own XML does not yet imply compliance with the SCP-ECG or DICOM standards—their implementation will require separate development.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Making the program resilient to errors
blocks.html:
The program receives, displays and saves the ECG, but connection errors, packet corruption, insufficient free space or unexpected application termination may occur during operation.

Such failures can lead to the loss of medical information or create a false impression that the study is complete.

We therefore provide error checking at every stage of processing.

If the connection is lost, the program saves the data already received and marks the study as interrupted. If a packet is corrupted, it records an integrity violation, and if saving is impossible, it reports the cause of the error.

After restarting, the program checks unfinished studies and does not present them as complete recordings.

Software errors now become detectable and should not alter medical information unnoticed.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Testing the computer application
blocks.html:
We have created a program that combines data acquisition, ECG display, HR calculation, archiving and report generation. However, each function must be tested while working together with the others.

We therefore connect the application to the training test bench and perform studies in sequence using ECG characteristics known in advance.

We check that a 30-second recording at a rate of 500 Hz contains 15 000 samples. We compare the displayed amplitude and HR with the simulator's parameters.

We then test changing the filters, saving the study in the database, reopening it and exporting it to CSV, PDF and XML. We pay particular attention to whether the raw data match before and after saving.

We separately reproduce communication disruptions and write errors.

As a result, we obtain a laboratory hardware and software system capable of recording an artificial ECG, displaying it and saving studies.

Medical information can now be used on a standalone computer. However, remote interaction with a physician requires that it be transferred beyond the local application.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Data transmission and integration with telemedicine
Moving to wireless ECG transmission
blocks.html:
We have learned to transfer the ECG from the device to a computer via USB. However, a wired connection limits the use of a portable electrocardiograph and requires external equipment to be connected.

We therefore use the Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) technology built into the ESP32-S3—a wireless connection with low power consumption.

In the ESP-IDF firmware, we enable the NimBLE stack, which allows the ESP32-S3 to exchange data via Bluetooth. The device will transmit digital measurements, and the computer or smartphone will receive them.

The electrocardiograph can now transmit information without a USB cable. This eliminates the need for a wired connection to the computer during wireless transmission, but does not replace patient protection within the device itself.
blocks.author: ai_checked
