blocks.title: Creating a wireless ECG transmission channel
blocks.html:
Bluetooth allows a connection to be established between the device and a computer, but we need to define what information will be transmitted and how the receiving program will recognize it.

For this, we use GATT—a mechanism for organizing data exchange in Bluetooth LE.

On the ESP32-S3, we create our own ECG GATT service with a unique UUID identifier. Within it, we provide an ECG Data characteristic for transmitting samples, Control for commands to start and stop recording, and Status for obtaining the device's status.

For ECG Data, we use Notify notifications, which allow the device to send new data to the connected computer.

The wireless connection now has a specific purpose: to transmit the ECG and control recording. However, the integrity of the incoming data must be ensured.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Ensuring continuity of wireless transmission
blocks.html:
At a sampling rate of 500 Hz, the device acquires 500 samples every second. If each raw sample occupies 3 bytes, 1500 bytes per second must be transmitted, excluding overhead information.

However, Bluetooth transmits data in separate packets whose size is limited by the negotiated connection parameters.

We therefore combine several samples into one packet. In its header, we specify the study identifier, the number of the first sample, the number of values and the packet number. We choose the size based on the negotiated ATT MTU.

Since a Bluetooth notification alone does not confirm that the application has saved the data, we provide checks of the received numbers and retransmission of missing segments from the device's memory.

Temporary communication delays should now not lead to unnoticed loss of medical information.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Connecting a computer to the ECG device via Bluetooth
blocks.html:
The electrocardiograph transmits measurements via Bluetooth, but the Windows program we developed currently receives data only via USB.

To use wireless communication, we add the Bleak library to the Python application, allowing it to connect to Bluetooth LE devices.

The program detects our device by its identifier, establishes a connection through BleakClient and subscribes to notifications from the ECG Data characteristic using start_notify().

The received packets are sent to the module we have already created for reconstructing the sample sequence. As a result, plot display, HR calculation and study saving continue to work without changes.

The application can now receive an ECG via either USB or Bluetooth. However, the data remain on the connected computer, while a physician may need remote access to the study.

blocks.title: Enabling network connectivity via Wi-Fi
blocks.html:
Bluetooth enables ECG transmission to a nearby computer, but does not allow the study to be sent independently to a remote medical server.

For this, we can use the computer's internet connection or the Wi-Fi module built into the ESP32-S3.

In the ESP-IDF firmware, we provide a Wi-Fi Station (STA) mode in which the device connects to an authorized wireless network. To transmit completed studies, we use HTTPS through the esp_http_client component with server certificate verification.

Network operations are performed separately from ADC sample acquisition so that Wi-Fi delays do not disrupt recording.

Thus, a study can reach a remote system either through a computer or directly from the device. However, its delivery must be ensured even if the internet connection is temporarily lost.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Ensuring study delivery over an unstable connection
blocks.html:
The device can transmit an ECG via Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, but the internet connection may be interrupted before the study has finished uploading.

If the data are deleted immediately after transmission begins, some medical information may be lost.

We therefore first save the completed study in the device's or computer's memory and then place it in the transmission queue.

After a successful upload, the server must confirm receipt of the complete file. Until confirmation, the study remains stored locally. If the connection is interrupted, the program retransmits the missing data.

To check integrity, we calculate a SHA-256 checksum and compare it on the sending and receiving sides.

A temporary loss of connection should now not lead to the loss of a study. However, delivery confirmation requires a server capable of receiving, checking and storing medical data.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Creating an ECG storage server
blocks.html:
Until now, study results have been saved on the device or computer. However, remote access for a physician requires a centralized repository accessible over a network.

We therefore develop a server application in Python using FastAPI.

When a new study arrives, the server creates a record with a unique identifier. We save the metadata in PostgreSQL and the raw digital signal in separate file or object storage.

For data exchange, we create an API: POST /api/studies to register a study and PUT /api/studies/{id}/signal to upload its signal. Through GET /api/studies/{id}, the program will be able to obtain information about the saved record.

The server checks data integrity and prevents duplicate studies from being created when the same identifier is sent again.

The ECG can now be stored centrally and remain accessible independently of the computer on which the measurement was performed.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Linking a transmitted study to a patient
blocks.html:
Saved ECGs are appearing on the server, but medical use requires reliable identification of the patient to whom each recording belongs.

We have already created patient and study identifiers in the computer application. We now need to preserve this link when transferring data to the server.

When uploading a study, we transmit the patient ID, study ID, device ID, recording time and measurement parameters. The server checks that the corresponding patient record exists and verifies the sending party's permissions.

If the identifier is unknown or the information is inconsistent, the study must not be automatically added to someone else's medical history.

The received ECG can now become part of a particular patient's study history. However, centralized storage of medical information creates a need to protect it from unauthorized access.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Protecting medical data
blocks.html:
Remote storage allows a physician to obtain an ECG regardless of the patient's location, but also creates a risk of unauthorized acquisition or modification of medical information.

We therefore organize access to the server through authentication and differentiated user permissions. A physician can view studies for patients they are authorized to access, while technical staff must not automatically gain access to the studies' medical content.

We protect transmission between the computer and the server using HTTPS with TLS. For Bluetooth, we provide secure pairing and connection encryption. Stored medical data must also be protected.

We record all access to studies in an audit log.

Thus, ensuring a person's safety extends to preserving the integrity and confidentiality of information about their health. We can now provide an authorized physician with access to the studies.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Enabling remote ECG viewing by a physician
blocks.html:
The server stores studies and protects them from unauthorized access, but the medical purpose is achieved not by saving the data itself, but by making it possible to use them to assess the condition of the heart.

We therefore create a physician's web interface that interacts with the server through an API.

After authorization, the physician selects a patient and opens that patient's study. The system displays the ECG, recording time, HR, filtering parameters and signal quality information.

For detailed examination, we provide zoom controls, viewing of individual segments and switching between the raw and processed signals.

The physician can add a conclusion, which is saved separately from the original ECG together with information about its author and the time it was written.

Medical information now becomes available for remote analysis, but interaction with other medical systems requires that it be represented in generally accepted formats.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Converting ECG data to medical exchange formats
blocks.html:
Our server stores digital measurements and provides them through its own API. However, other medical systems may use different formats for representing ECGs.

We therefore provide for converting the study into SCP-ECG and DICOM, as specified in the technical specification.

To do this, we retain the exact sample values, sampling rate, lead information, voltage units, and measurement device characteristics. These data must be converted into the structure of the corresponding standard without altering the original recording.

Since our device records only one lead, for DICOM we consider the applicable General ECG Waveform format rather than presenting the recording as a standard 12-lead ECG.

We check compatibility with the specific medical system that will receive the data.

The measurement results can now be represented not only in our own format, but also in formats intended for medical data exchange.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Integrating the electrocardiograph with a medical information system
blocks.html:
Standardized formats allow an ECG recording to be transmitted, but full interaction with a medical information system (MIS) also requires coordination of information about the patient, the study, and its result.

We therefore develop an integration API through which the MIS can obtain information about the ECG and a link to its original recording.

The HL7 FHIR standard can be used for implementation. In it, the Patient resource represents the patient, Observation represents the measurement result, and DiagnosticReport allows results to be combined into a study. With an appropriate profile, the sequence of ECG values can be represented through SampledData.

We agree on the specific exchange structure according to the requirements of the MIS being connected.

The ECG now becomes part of the electronic medical document workflow rather than a separate file that has to be transferred manually.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Providing remote ECG interpretation
blocks.html:
Transmitting the study to the MIS makes the ECG available to a physician, but the medical information must be interpreted in light of the patient's condition and the limitations of the measurement itself.

We therefore provide for remote ECG interpretation by a physician. The physician examines the recording, assesses its quality, and prepares a report.

The technical specification also permits the use of artificial intelligence. For this purpose, a separate module can be developed to identify possible rhythm disturbances and suggest sections of the ECG recording for the physician to review.

However, the AI algorithm must undergo independent clinical validation. Until this is completed, its results cannot be used as a standalone medical diagnosis.

Thus, remote processing expands the possibilities for obtaining information about heart function, but also requires checks on the reliability of medical conclusions.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Testing the complete telemedicine study process
blocks.html:
We have implemented ECG transmission, server storage, a medical archive, and remote physician access. However, correct operation of each component on its own does not yet guarantee reliable transmission of the study from the device to the medical system.

We therefore carry out an end-to-end test on the training test bench.

The simulator reproduces an ECG at 60 beats per minute. The device records 30 seconds of the signal at a sampling rate of 500 Hz and saves 15 000 samples.

We transmit the study via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, upload it to the server, and open it in the physician's interface. We compare the original samples with those received on the server and check that the measurement parameters match.

We then simulate a connection failure, resending the file, and an access attempt without the necessary permissions.

As a result, we obtain a remote ECG transmission system tested with an artificial signal, in which preservation of medical information is accompanied by integrity and access checks.

However, practical use requires combining the electronic components into a protected portable device and confirming the safety of its design.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Creating the enclosure and portable device
Moving from separate electronic assemblies to a single device
blocks.html:
On the training test bench, electronic components can be positioned separately from one another. However, for a portable ECG device, they must form a single structure that can be carried and used without disrupting the electrical connections.

To achieve this, we need to determine the relative positions of the measurement board, microcontroller, rechargeable battery, and external interfaces.

We begin with the device layout—determining the positions of the electronic assemblies inside the future enclosure. We use the actual dimensions of the developed boards, the positions of their connectors, and the requirements for electrical connections.

In FreeCAD, we create a preliminary three-dimensional model of the device. The geometry of the printed circuit boards can be transferred from KiCad in STEP format.

In this way, the separate electronic assemblies begin to form a single spatial structure. However, positioning them close together may increase the mutual influence of their electrical circuits.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Positioning the electronic assemblies without disrupting measurements
blocks.html:
Combining the measurement signal chain and digital electronics reduces the size of the device, but creates a risk of interference entering the weak ECG signal.

The influence of the ESP32-S3 microcontroller is particularly significant because its digital circuits and wireless module generate high-frequency electrical effects.

We therefore position the sensitive ADS1291 measurement signal chain separately from sources of digital interference when arranging the components. We keep the input connections short and maintain an area around the ESP32-S3 antenna free of interfering metal structures, in accordance with the module manufacturer's requirements.

We secure the boards on the designated mounting supports, preventing accidental contact between their conductive parts and other structural elements.

The electronic assemblies can now operate within a confined space. However, the enclosure itself must protect not only the electronics from external influences, but also the person from dangerous electrical contact.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Creating a protective enclosure for the device
blocks.html:
Electronic boards contain conductive areas under electrical voltage. While they remain accessible from outside, accidental contact or the entry of foreign objects can disrupt the device's operation and create a hazard.

We therefore provide an enclosure made of electrically insulating material that covers the internal electronic components.

For the preliminary design, we consider polycarbonate or a suitable PC/ABS plastic. We select the specific material with regard to mechanical strength, fire performance, cleaning conditions, and applicable medical safety requirements.

The enclosure must prevent accidental access to conductive parts, but the plastic shell alone does not provide all the necessary protection for the patient against leakage currents.

Electrical insulation and protection of the measurement input must therefore be considered together with the enclosure design and checked against the applicable requirements of IEC 60601-1.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Creating a protected connection to the electrodes
blocks.html:
The enclosure covers the electronic components, but the ECG signal must enter the device from outside. The measurement input must therefore be brought out to an accessible connector.

An ordinary electrical connection is not suitable for a medical device: it must ensure reliable contact, prevent incorrect connection, and withstand mechanical stresses during use.

We therefore provide a specialized patient cable connector compatible with the selected electrode system and the design of the protected measurement input.

We secure the connector in the enclosure so that force from the cable is not transmitted directly to the sensitive connections of the measurement board. We protect the contact parts from accidental touch in accordance with the requirements for the medical device.

On the training test bench, we check the mechanical reliability of the connection and the cable's influence on the recorded signal.

The measurement system can now receive an external signal through a protected interface. However, a rechargeable battery remains inside the enclosure, and its placement also affects the device's safety.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Securing the rechargeable battery inside the enclosure
blocks.html:
The rechargeable battery allows the ECG device to operate independently, but is subjected to mechanical stresses when the device is carried.

If the battery shifts, this can disrupt electrical connections or damage its casing. We therefore provide a separate mounting location inside the enclosure for the protected battery module.

The design must prevent the module from moving and eliminate dangerous mechanical pressure from other components. We position the battery with regard to permissible temperatures, the manufacturer's requirements, and the possibility of servicing it.

To power the electronic assemblies, we retain the previously developed voltage regulation and charge control system.

The battery now becomes part of a single structure and allows it to operate independently. However, replenishing its energy requires bringing the charging interface outside without compromising the enclosure's protective properties.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Providing access to the charging connector
blocks.html:
The rechargeable battery is positioned inside the enclosure, but after it is discharged, the device must receive energy from an external source.

We therefore bring the USB-C connector required by the technical specification out to the enclosure and connect it to the battery charging system we have developed.

We position it so that connecting the cable does not place a mechanical load on the printed circuit board. However, connection to external equipment can create additional paths for electrical effects on the measurement system.

We therefore provide a hardware interlock that prevents measurements during charging. Software control by the ESP32-S3 must additionally monitor the USB-C connection status, but does not replace hardware protection.

The device can now be charged without opening the enclosure, but the user must understand when it is charging, ready for operation, or indicating a malfunction.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Creating controls and indicators
blocks.html:
We have placed the electronic components inside the enclosure, but the user cannot directly observe their operation.

To start and stop a study, we provide a control button connected to the ESP32-S3 microcontroller.

However, one button is not enough: the user must be able to distinguish the device's readiness from recording, charging, and malfunction states.

We therefore place firmware-controlled indicator lights on the enclosure. They must show the power status, recording in progress, low battery charge, and detected errors.

We provide protection against accidental button presses and check that the indications correspond to the device's actual state.

The user can now control the device without accessing the internal electronic components. However, their combined operation inside the closed enclosure generates heat, which must be taken into account.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Ensuring acceptable thermal operating conditions
blocks.html:
During operation, electronic components consume energy, some of which is converted into heat. Once they are placed in a closed enclosure, heat dissipation conditions change.

It is particularly important to account for heating of the ESP32-S3 during wireless transmission and of the battery during charging.

We therefore investigate the device's thermal operating conditions. On the training test bench, we measure component temperatures during prolonged recording, data transmission, and battery charging.

Based on the results, we determine whether it is necessary to change the component arrangement, use heat-conducting elements, or restrict operating modes.

The enclosure surface must not reach unacceptable temperatures, and the temperature conditions must meet the requirements for the battery and medical equipment.

The design now accounts not only for the electrical interaction between components, but also for the thermal consequences of their combined operation.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Manufacturing and assembling the prototype enclosure
blocks.html:
We have determined the arrangement of the electronic components, the methods for securing them, and the necessary external interfaces. However, the computer model does not yet allow us to establish how conveniently and reliably they can be combined into an actual device.

We therefore manufacture a prototype enclosure from the prepared model, for example by 3D printing.

Inside it, we secure the printed circuit boards and protected battery module and install the designated connectors, button, and indicators. We check that the dimensions match, that there is no mechanical pressure on the components, and that the mountings are reliable.

The assembled enclosure must allow the intended cleaning, and its external surfaces must not have dangerous sharp projections.

If discrepancies are found during assembly, we revise the three-dimensional model and repeat the manufacturing process.

The previously separate electronic processes now acquire a shared physical structure—a portable electrocardiograph prototype.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Checking the device's dimensions, mass, and battery life
blocks.html:
The assembled device performs the intended electrical functions, but its portability has not yet been confirmed. Increasing battery capacity extends operating time while also increasing the device's dimensions and mass.

We therefore measure the prototype's mass and overall dimensions, then determine its battery life during ECG recording and data transmission.

To do this, we use the fully charged device on the training test bench, recording the operating time until the control system ends recording because of low charge, as intended.

If battery life proves insufficient, we reconsider the components' power consumption, the wireless transmission mode, and the battery module's characteristics.

According to the technical specification, the final requirements for battery life, mass, and overall dimensions still need to be established.

Portability now becomes a verifiable characteristic of the device rather than merely a feature of its design.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Testing the combined operation of the assembled device
blocks.html:
We have placed the measurement signal chain, controller, battery, and controls in a single enclosure. However, assembly may have changed the conditions for electrical measurement, component cooling, and wireless communication.

We therefore return to the training test bench and repeat the recording of a known ECG signal.

We set the simulator to 60 beats per minute and an amplitude of 1 mV. The device must make a 30-second recording at a sampling rate of 500 Hz, saving 15 000 consecutive samples.

We check the measured amplitude, waveform, heart rate (HR) calculation, interference level, study storage, and data transmission. We separately investigate battery-powered operation, the measurement interlock during charging, error indications, and the stability of wireless communication inside the enclosure.

As a result, we obtain a physically assembled portable prototype of a single-channel ECG device capable of performing the intended measurements on the training test bench.

However, the prototype's functionality does not yet prove that it is safe for people. The next process therefore becomes a comprehensive check of accuracy, reliability, and compliance with medical requirements.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Testing, confirmation of safety, and compliance with the technical specification
Defining the conditions for testing the completed electrocardiograph
blocks.html:
We have assembled a portable single-channel ECG device, but correct operation of the individual components does not yet prove that the device as a whole is suitable for medical purposes.

To establish this, we need to check how closely its actual characteristics meet the requirements of the technical specification.

We begin by defining acceptance criteria—measurable indicators used to establish whether the device has fulfilled its assigned task.

According to the technical specification, the characteristics of the electrical signal, heart rate (HR) accuracy, noise level, filtering, data transmission, electrode lead-off detection, and safety must be checked.

However, the technical specification does not establish all the necessary numerical limits, particularly permissible noise, input impedance, and CMRR. We therefore clarify these requirements before final testing, taking into account the device's intended medical use.

The device's functionality can now be assessed not merely by whether an ECG recording appears, but by compliance with the established characteristics.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Checking the accuracy of electrical voltage measurement
blocks.html:
An ECG device obtains information about the heart by measuring electrical voltage. However, even when the ECG trace has the correct shape, the voltage values may differ from the actual values.

We therefore use a training test bench with a calibrated ECG simulator that generates a signal with a known amplitude.

First, we set the amplitude to 1 mV, record the signal and compare the result with the set value. We then repeat the measurement at other amplitudes, checking whether accuracy is maintained across the required range.

At the same time, we check whether the ADC is overloaded and how the result changes at different gain settings.

Since the input impedance of the measurement chain affects the voltage received from the electrodes, we also check this characteristic using specialized laboratory equipment.

We can now establish not only the presence of an ECG signal, but also the accuracy with which its electrical characteristics are measured.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Checking the accuracy of signal recording over time
blocks.html:
Accurate voltage measurement does not yet guarantee a correct ECG, since information about the heart's function also depends on the duration and sequence of electrical processes.

We therefore check the sampling rate and continuity of recording.

On the training test bench, we set a known periodic signal and make a 30-second recording at a frequency of 500 Hz. This should produce 15 000 consecutive samples.

Using an independent means of monitoring time, we check the actual measurement frequency, and use the sample numbers to identify missing or repeated samples.

We also confirm that the ADC provides the specified 24-bit representation of measurements. Actual accuracy is assessed separately, since bit depth alone does not determine the noise level.

The recording should now correctly reproduce not only changes in voltage, but also their sequence over time.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Checking intrinsic noise and suppression of electrical interference
blocks.html:
We have confirmed voltage and time measurement, but the weak ECG signal may be distorted by the device's intrinsic noise and external electrical influences.

To determine the intrinsic noise of the measurement chain, we use the test mode provided in the ADC documentation. We record the resulting values and calculate the root mean square noise level (RMS) within the specified frequency band.

We then check the device's ability to suppress common-mode interference—interference that affects both measurement inputs equally. This ability is characterized by the CMRR ratio.

We perform the tests using specialized measurement equipment, without connecting a person.

We compare the measured noise and CMRR values with the criteria established for medical use of the device.

It is now possible to determine how well the measurement system can distinguish the weak ECG signal from electrical interference.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Checking the effect of filtering on the ECG trace
blocks.html:
Suppressing electrical interference produces a cleaner signal, but software filters may also change the shape of the ECG trace itself.

It is therefore necessary to check not only the effectiveness of interference removal, but also the preservation of useful medical information.

On the training test bench, we reproduce signals with known frequency characteristics and check the effects of the high-pass, low-pass and mains interference filters.

We separately compare the original and processed ECG, determining how filtering affects the amplitude, time intervals and shape of characteristic portions of the signal.

We check whether the filters can be disabled and the original samples saved regardless of the selected processing mode.

Interference reduction now becomes a controlled process that should not lead to unacceptable distortion of medical information.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Checking HR calculation and fault detection
blocks.html:
The device records changes in the electrical activity of the heart and calculates its rate of contraction. However, an error in detecting cardiac cycles may lead to an incorrect assessment of a person's condition.

For testing, we use an ECG simulator that successively reproduces heart rates of 60, 90 and 120 beats per minute.

We compare the calculated HR with the set values and determine the measurement error. We then reproduce interference and loss of electrode contact using the test bench's permitted means.

We check whether the device detects deterioration in signal quality, warns the user and stops providing unreliable HR values.

The results allow us to assess how correctly the system distinguishes actual changes in heart rhythm from measurement errors.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Checking the preservation and transmission of medical information
blocks.html:
We have confirmed that a digital ECG can be obtained, but storing and transmitting data may result in loss, corruption or incorrect association of an examination with a patient.

We therefore perform an end-to-end check of medical data integrity.

First, we save the original recording in the device's memory. We then transfer it via USB, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, upload it to a server and retrieve it again for analysis.

We compare the number of samples, their values, timing characteristics and checksums. We also check that the CSV and XML files and the PDF report match the original data.

We then simulate a connection failure and retransmission of the examination. We check that the data are not lost, duplicated or associated with another patient.

ECG transmission now becomes a verifiable continuation of measurement rather than an independent source of unreliable information.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Checking battery life and structural robustness
blocks.html:
Electronic measurements may be accurate on a laboratory test bench, but placing the components in a portable enclosure introduces additional operating conditions.

During recording, battery energy is consumed, electronic components heat up, and movement of the device creates mechanical stresses.

We therefore check battery life, power supply stability, temperature conditions and structural reliability.

On the TTB, we perform prolonged recording of an artificial ECG while monitoring the battery condition and signal quality. We separately check the provided measurement lockout during charging via USB-C.

We conduct mechanical tests of the enclosure and connectors according to a predefined program, then repeat the measurement checks.

We now determine whether the portable device maintains the required characteristics not only under ideal laboratory conditions, but also under the intended operating conditions.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Assessing the risks of using the electrocardiograph
blocks.html:
The previous tests allow specific faults to be detected, but medical safety also requires consideration of hazardous situations that have not yet occurred during testing.

We therefore perform a risk analysis in accordance with ISO 14971.

We investigate the possible consequences of an electrical fault, signal loss, incorrect HR calculation, overheating, a software error or unreliable transmission of medical data.

For each hazardous situation, we identify possible harm, assess the risk and establish measures to reduce it. We then check the effectiveness of these measures and assess the risk that remains after they are applied.

If the residual risk does not meet the established acceptability criteria, the design or software must be changed.

Thus, ensuring safety becomes a continuous process of assessing and limiting risks that accompanies the creation and subsequent use of the medical device.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Confirming the device's electrical safety
blocks.html:
The risk analysis shows that the possibility of a dangerous electric current passing through a person's body is particularly important for a contact ECG device.

It is therefore necessary to check whether the protective measures provided by the design actually prevent unacceptable electrical effects.

To do this, we arrange testing according to the applicable requirements of IEC 60601-1, which establishes general requirements for the basic safety and essential performance of medical electrical equipment.

A specialized testing laboratory checks electrical insulation, leakage currents, accessible parts of the device, and safety under normal operation and specified single faults. The required type of protection for the part of the device that contacts the patient is determined beforehand.

If testing reveals nonconformities, the protective design is revised and tested again.

Only documented confirmation of electrical safety allows further medical use of the device to be considered. Battery operation alone is no substitute for this confirmation.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Checking immunity to external electrical influences
blocks.html:
The device's electrical safety is not limited to its own currents and voltages. In a medical environment, it may be exposed to electromagnetic interference and other external influences.

For example, electronic devices operating nearby can disrupt measurement of the weak ECG signal. It is therefore necessary to confirm the device's electromagnetic compatibility (EMC).

Testing according to IEC 60601-1-2 allows assessment of the device's immunity to specified electromagnetic influences and the level of interference it generates.

In addition, the technical specification requires defibrillator protection. Its presence and effectiveness are checked by a specialized laboratory according to the applicable requirements for this type of electrocardiograph, without conducting hazardous tests on an ordinary training test bench.

After exposure, we check that the required safety and specified performance are maintained.

The device should thus provide reliable ECG recording not only in the absence of interference, but also in the specified electromagnetic environment.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Checking the safety of materials and conditions of use
blocks.html:
Even with confirmed electrical safety, a medical device may cause harm because of the properties of materials that contact the body or because of improper conditions of use.

We therefore check the safety of the electrodes, contact materials, and intended methods of using and cleaning the device.

To assess the biological safety of components that contact the skin, we apply ISO 10993-1, taking into account the nature and duration of contact.

If the device is intended for home use, we also consider the requirements of IEC 60601-1-11. The design and instructions must account for the possibility that the device will be used by a person without specialized medical training.

Based on these requirements, we refine the materials, labeling, warnings and permissible operating conditions.

Safety is now considered not only as protection against electricity, but also as a property of the entire interaction between a person and the medical device.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Confirming software safety
blocks.html:
The hardware may measure the ECG correctly, but a software error can alter the signal, calculate HR incorrectly or transmit an unreliable examination to the physician.

It is therefore necessary to confirm the reliability of the software throughout its development and subsequent use.

To do this, we apply the requirements of IEC 62304 for the life cycle of medical device software.

We document the requirements for each software module, specify its version and its relationship to the implemented functions. We then perform unit and integration tests, checking signal processing, communication errors, data storage and recovery after failures.

We separately check the protection of medical information, access rights and resistance to unauthorized data modification.

The reliability of the ECG now depends not only on the accuracy of electronic measurement, but also on the confirmed correctness of software processing.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Confirming the medical suitability of ECG results
blocks.html:
We have checked the device's technical accuracy and safety, but this is not yet sufficient to claim that the information obtained can address the stated medical tasks.

It is therefore necessary to establish the medical suitability of the measurement results.

Our device records one ECG lead for 10–30 seconds. Such a recording allows certain characteristics of heart rhythm to be examined, but does not replace a standard diagnostic 12-lead ECG.

First, we determine exactly which medical tasks the device is intended for: rhythm recording, screening for specific disorders or obtaining a diagnostic conclusion.

We then select the applicable particular standards and conduct the necessary clinical evaluation. IEC 60601-2-25 applies to electrocardiographs for diagnostic recordings, while IEC 60601-2-47 applies to ambulatory systems for continuous recording and analysis, so it cannot automatically be extended to short-duration ECG recording.

The technical capability to measure is thus compared with actual medical usefulness and the established limits of use.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Preparing the medical device for registration and use
blocks.html:
Even if the tests performed confirm measurement accuracy and device safety, medical use requires documented confirmation of compliance with the established requirements.

We therefore compile a technical dossier for the medical device, bringing together the design description, circuit diagrams, software documentation, test results, risk analysis and operating documentation.

For Kazakhstan, we determine the device's risk class and the applicable state registration procedure. Within the EAEU, medical devices can continue to be registered under either EAEU rules or the national rules of the member states until 31 December 2027.

After the necessary expert opinions have been obtained and the required registration procedures completed, the device may be authorized for medical use within the established limits.

Thus, checking functionality, confirming safety and obtaining state registration complete the transformation of a laboratory prototype into a medical device intended to obtain information about the function of the human heart.
blocks.author: ai_checked

blocks.title: Qualitative leap—creating a single-channel electrocardiograph
blocks.html:
We began by creating a way to obtain reliable information about the function of the human heart for medical purposes. This required measuring the electrical activity of the heart, but electrical interaction between the device and a person may pose a danger to their health.

A contradiction arose: ensuring a person's safety requires obtaining information about the heart's function using ECG and, at the same time, limits the use of ECG because of a possible electrical hazard.

During assembly, we created a training test bench, a measurement chain, and a power supply and electrical protection system, and developed software, data processing and transmission. Each of these processes enabled information about the heart to be obtained while limiting risks to the person.

The qualitative leap is the creation of a single-channel electrocardiograph in which measuring the electrical activity of the heart and ensuring a person's safety are combined into a single process of obtaining reliable medical information.

The contradiction thus receives a practical resolution: electrical measurement is not eliminated, but becomes possible under specially created and verified safety conditions.

However, creating a functioning prototype does not yet mean that the resolution of the contradiction is complete. Medical use requires confirmation of the device's accuracy, safety and compliance with the established requirements.

The resulting electrocardiograph becomes a new starting process whose further development opens up opportunities to improve the accuracy, safety and accessibility of heart examinations.
blocks.author: ai_checked
